$comment: Entries added after the original workbook import. Written by the /toolbox-add skill or by hand — see .claude/skills/toolbox-add/SKILL.md for the schema and the house rules. Everything here carries an addedAt, which is what drives the Newly added section.

entries.name: posts.design
entries.takeaway: A hand-picked wall of social post design — 378 captures of product updates, announcements and launches from X, browsable by recency or by brand, each keeping its creator, platform and original link. Run by one curator (@baseddesigner) whose stated filter is what is worth stealing rather than what spreads.
entries.whatToDo: Reference, not a dependency. Open it when designing a launch or announcement post for a client or for Gitwork, take the structure and the hierarchy, and leave the styling behind. Anything genuinely good gets screenshotted into the Foundry wiki rather than relied on staying up.
entries.cost: Free. No ads and no paywall; the curator asks for voluntary tips.
notes: Narrow but real: announcement and launch post design is a surface we produce for nearly every client, and there is no decent reference for it beyond scrolling a feed. It is inspiration only — no product, no export, no API, nothing to install.

Same IP caution as Flaude and Refero Styles. These are other companies' posts and trade dress. Fine as internal reference; a problem if a layout or a line of copy survives into a client deliverable, so treat it as structure-only input.

One person, no company, free by choice with tips — assume it can disappear. /pricing and /submit both returned 500 when requested directly, so free-forever is the curator's current position rather than a commitment, and takedowns are handled by DM.

entries.name: shadcn/ui
entries.what: Not a component dependency — a registry you copy Radix-and-Tailwind component source out of, into your own repo, where you then own and edit it. Ships blocks, charts, a theming layer and a CLI that writes the files.
entries.priceDetail: Free. MIT-licensed, no accounts, no paid tier.
notes: The default answer for a React UI layer on client work: because the code lands in the repo rather than in node_modules, there is no upgrade treadmill and no vendor to outlive. It is also what most coding agents already know, so an agent asked for 'a dialog' produces something that matches the rest of the codebase.

Copy-in cuts both ways — you inherit maintenance of every component you pull, and there is no `npm update` to pick up upstream fixes. Worth pinning the registry version you generated from in the project README.
121k GitHub stars showing on the site. Effectively the industry default, which is the real argument for standardising on it rather than on anything more novel.

entries.name: 21st.dev
entries.what: Marketplace of 12,000+ React and Tailwind components, templates and shadcn themes — 2,000+ marketing blocks, 2,100+ UI components — with an MCP endpoint and CLI so an agent can search and install a component without leaving the editor.
entries.priceDetail: The site is browsable without an account. Plan table lists three paid tiers and no free tier: Builder $6/mo, Builder + AI $15/mo (500–2,000 AI credits, top-ups +100 for $5, credits roll over), Team $7.50/seat/mo for 2–50 seats. All figures billed yearly; quarterly is dearer.
notes: The MCP endpoint is the reason to care. Unlimited component retrieval via MCP on any paid tier means an agent building a marketing page pulls real components instead of inventing markup — which is where most agent-built pages fall apart.
Marketplace, not a library: quality varies by contributor, so it wants review before anything reaches a client site. There is no single maintainer standing behind an individual component.

The 21st AI half (multi-model generation, sandbox code mode) is a separate product from the marketplace and priced by credits. Buy the marketplace tier for the components; do not assume the AI credits are worth the difference until someone has tested them.

entries.name: React Bits
entries.what: Collection of animated, interactive React components — text effects, backgrounds, transitions — offered in JS and TS variants with and without Tailwind, copied in by hand or via a CLI.
entries.priceDetail: Free. Licensed MIT + Commons Clause: commercial use of the components in a product is allowed, selling or redistributing the components themselves is not.
notes: Read the licence before shipping. MIT + Commons Clause permits use in client sites and products, but forbids selling, sublicensing or redistributing the components alone, in a bundle, or as a port — so these must not end up inside a Gitwork starter kit or template we hand on or resell.
45,443 stars and a push yesterday, but a single maintainer (David Haz). Fine for copy-in components, where a stalled repo costs us nothing.
Best-in-class for the decorative layer — the text reveals and background effects a landing page needs — which is exactly the work that otherwise eats a day of hand-rolled motion code.

entries.name: Fancy Components
entries.what: Copy-in React components and microinteractions built on Motion and Tailwind — physics-driven text, cursor effects, elastic drags. Deliberately over-the-top rather than a general-purpose UI kit.
entries.priceDetail: Free. MIT licence.
notes: MIT means no restriction on reuse in our own starters, unlike React Bits — worth knowing when picking which library a Gitwork template pulls from.
3,073 stars and last pushed 2026-03-14, so about five months quiet at the time of adding. Copy-in code, so a stalled repo is a low risk; treat anything you copy as ours to maintain.
One person (Daniel Petho). Use it for a specific effect a page needs, not as the foundation of a design system.

entries.name: Motion Primitives
entries.what: Copy-in motion components for React built on Motion and Tailwind — animated lists, dialogs, cursors, text effects — aimed at the layer between a component library and hand-written animation code.
entries.priceDetail: Free. MIT licence.
notes: Assessed from the GitHub repo, not the docs site: motion-primitives.com returned 429 behind a Vercel security checkpoint on every attempt, so nobody here has read the component docs yet. Open it in a browser before relying on it.

The repo states 'This project is in beta. Expect new components to be released regularly and significant updates to the code.' Copy-in code from a beta project means breaking changes are our problem, not an upgrade path.
5,952 stars, MIT, last pushed 2026-03-19 — same five-month quiet spell as Fancy Components, same single-maintainer profile (ibelick).

entries.name: Anime.js
entries.what: General-purpose JavaScript animation engine — timelines, springs, scroll-linked animation, SVG morphing, WAAPI output — driven from one API rather than tied to a framework.
entries.priceDetail: Free. MIT licence (animejs 4.5.0 on npm).
notes: v4 is a full rewrite and is MIT-licensed on npm, which matters because v4 spent time as sponsorware and older write-ups still say it is paid. Check the licence field, not the blog posts.
The reason to reach for it over Motion: it is framework-agnostic, so it covers the Webflow, Framer-embed and plain-HTML work where a React-only motion library is no use.
Effectively one maintainer (Julian Garnier) on a library used everywhere. Low risk — it is a build-time dependency with no service behind it.

entries.name: NumberFlow
entries.what: One component that animates a number changing — digit-by-digit transitions with correct formatting via Intl.NumberFormat, dependency-free, screen-reader friendly. React, Vue and Svelte builds.
entries.priceDetail: Free. MIT licence (@number-flow/react 0.6.2 on npm).
notes: Narrow on purpose, and worth it: animated counters and price toggles appear on nearly every landing page and dashboard we build, and hand-rolled ones almost always break tabular alignment, currency formatting or the accessibility tree. This gets all three right.
Accessible by default — it renders a plain number for assistive tech and animates only the visual layer. That is the part a weekend build gets wrong.
Single maintainer (Maxwell Barvian), 7.6k on GitHub. It is a small MIT dependency with no service attached, so the downside of it going quiet is that we vendor it.

entries.name: Rive
entries.what: Editor plus runtimes for interactive vector animation: build a state machine in the editor, export a .riv file, drive it from code at runtime. Ships runtimes for web, iOS, Android, Flutter, React Native and game engines.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/seat (3 collaborative files, no .riv export). Cadet $9/seat/mo, 3 seats max, unlimited files and .riv export. Voyager $32/seat/mo, 25 seats max, adds Libraries and embed hosting. Enterprise $120/seat/mo above $10M revenue. Agent credits are extra: $20/seat/mo on Voyager, $40/seat/mo on Enterprise.
notes: The distinction that matters against Lottie: a .riv file carries a state machine, so the animation responds to input at runtime instead of playing a fixed sequence. That is how you ship a genuinely interactive illustration to both web and native from one asset.
Export is behind the paid tier — the free plan cannot produce a .riv — so any client project using Rive needs at least Cadet at $9/seat/mo from day one. Budget it, do not discover it.

Real production credibility (Spotify Wrapped, Duolingo). The cost is that the source of truth lives in Rive's editor rather than in our repo: whoever built the file owns it, and offboarding means re-authoring.

entries.name: Lottielab
entries.what: Browser editor for Lottie animations — import from Figma or SVG, animate, export .lottie/JSON, GIF or MP4, with hosting on a CDN. Aimed at product teams rather than After Effects animators.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier: unlimited files, Lottie and SVG upload, Figma import, GIF and MP4 export. Pro $12 per editor/month billed annually adds Lottie export, HD and 4K video, team library, comments, file-size optimisation and CDN hosting. Enterprise on request.
notes: Lottie export is the paid feature, and Lottie export is the entire point — the free tier is a viewer and a GIF exporter. Treat $12/editor/month as the real price of using it on client work.

The Figma import path is what makes it usable by a designer without After Effects, which is the gap it fills against Rive: simpler tool, dumber output. Lottie plays a fixed sequence and does not react to input.
Their CDN hosting is convenient and a dependency — a client site pulling a .lottie from Lottielab breaks if the account lapses. Self-host the file in the repo instead.

entries.name: Unicorn Studio
entries.what: Layer-based editor for real-time WebGL scenes — 75+ configurable effects, 3D models, extruded text and SVG, pointer and scroll interactivity — published as an embed or exported as JSON for its runtime. Layers rather than a shader node graph.
entries.priceDetail: Free: all 75+ effects, up to 8 publishes with Unicorn branding, personal and non-commercial use only. Legend $168/year or $20/mo: commercial licence, unlimited publishes with no watermark, JSON export, custom 3D models and fonts, versioning, 200 Unicorn AI credits a month.
notes: The free tier is explicitly personal and non-commercial. Any client scene needs Legend at $168/year — using the free plan on paid work is a licence breach, not a grey area.

Redistribution is prohibited on every plan, Legend included: we may use scenes in client deliverables, but we cannot bundle the Unicorn runtime into a Gitwork template or starter kit we hand on. That rules it out of anything productised.

The honest alternative to hand-written shaders for hero sections — a designer can build a gradient or fluid background in an afternoon that would otherwise be a week of GLSL. Watch the performance guide; these ship real GPU cost to mobile.

entries.name: Jitter
entries.what: Browser motion tool aimed at social and product marketing output — import Figma frames, animate on a simple timeline, export 4K video, GIF or Lottie. Templates rather than a blank canvas.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier: unlimited drafts, 3 workspace files, video/GIF/Lottie export capped at 720p 30fps, limited AI credits. Pro is priced per editor/month billed annually and Team above it — both figures render client-side and were not in the served page, so read them in-app before committing.
notes: Fills the gap between 'export a static frame from Figma' and 'open After Effects' for launch and announcement assets — the same surface posts.design covers as reference. 720p/30fps on the free tier means the free plan is for trying it, not shipping.
The Figma import is the whole workflow: it wants the design to exist already, which suits how we work and makes it useless as a design tool in its own right.
Pricing figures unverified — the tier structure is published but the numbers are injected by JavaScript. Do not quote a price to a client from this listing.

entries.name: tldraw
entries.what: Infinite-canvas SDK for React — the whiteboard at tldraw.com is the demo. Multiplayer sync, persistence and shape tooling included; also ships tldraw offline as a local app for you and your agents.
entries.priceDetail: tldraw.com is free to use. The SDK is free in development environments under the tldraw licence; production use needs a commercial licence with a licence key — 100-day free trial, then 'value-based pricing' by arrangement, no public figure.
notes: Read the licence before designing anything around it. The tldraw licence permits development, modification and bundling, but forbids production deployment without a key — a canvas feature demoed to a client on the trial becomes a sales conversation at launch, and the price is not published.

Where it earns its place is scope: multiplayer sync, undo, persistence and hit-testing on an infinite canvas are months of work, and this is the mature option. Used in production by Google, Shopify, Replit and Autodesk per their own site.
49,766 stars, pushed today, real company behind it (tldraw Inc). The free whiteboard is also the fastest way to sketch an architecture diagram with a client on a call — no signup, works on mobile.

entries.name: Paper
entries.what: Design tool built on web standards, pitched at teams shipping with agents — connects the canvas to code and data, and exposes a Paper MCP server so an agent can read and act on the design. Web app plus a desktop build.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0: unlimited viewers and editors, 100 MCP tool calls a week, limited image generation, 25MB image cap. Pro $16 per editor/month billed yearly ($20 monthly): 1M MCP calls a week, 100× image generation, video export, 100MB images. Organisations tier for SSO and custom contracts.
notes: Unusual and worth noting: editors are free, so a whole team can collaborate at $0 — the paywall is on MCP call volume and export, not on seats. That inverts Figma's model and makes it cheap to trial on a real project.
The MCP server is the actual pitch. If an agent can query the design directly, design-to-code stops being an export step. Whether that survives contact with a real build is untested here.
Young product against an entrenched incumbent, and the file format is theirs. Do not put a client's source of truth in it yet; use it where the output is code we own.

entries.name: Penpot
entries.what: Open-source design and prototyping platform, self-hostable, that works in SVG and CSS natively rather than in a proprietary format — so a developer can read the file's actual markup. Plugin API and libraries included.
entries.priceDetail: MPL-2.0 and self-hostable at no licence cost. Hosted plans list $0/user and $7/user/month tiers, with enterprise and support figures on the same page running up to $950/month.
notes: The reason it matters to us is data ownership, not features: self-hosted MPL-2.0 means a client's design files can live inside their own infrastructure, which is an answer we currently do not have for a client who will not put IP in Figma.
58,520 stars, pushed today, a real company and a funded roadmap — this is the credible open-source option, not a hobby project.
It is still behind Figma on polish and on the plugin ecosystem, and self-hosting means we operate it. Only worth proposing when the ownership requirement is real.

entries.name: Mobbin
entries.what: Searchable library of 400,000+ real app and web screenshots — 1,000+ iOS and web apps plus 200 sites — organised by flow (onboarding, paywall, empty state) and by UI element, with recorded animations on paid tiers.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier is capped at the latest 4 apps and 4 sites. Pro $10/month billed yearly (all apps, flows, animations, unlimited collections, screen downloads). Team $16 per member/month billed yearly. Finance+ add-on $399/month for 55+ finance apps.
notes: This is the pattern-research shortcut for client work: instead of arguing about how a paywall or an onboarding flow should behave, pull ten shipped examples in five minutes. $10/month is less than the time it saves on one project.
Free tier is a teaser — 4 apps. Assume Pro if anyone is going to actually use it.
Same IP caution as every reference library here: these are other companies' interfaces. Use them to inform structure and behaviour, never to lift layout or copy into a deliverable.

entries.name: OKLCH Colour Picker & Converter
entries.what: Picker and converter for OKLCH — paste a hex, RGB or HSL value and see it in perceptual colour space, with the sRGB gamut boundary drawn, the closest in-gamut fallback calculated, and a P3 preview. By Evil Martians (Andrey Sitnik and Roman Shamin).
entries.priceDetail: Free, no account.
notes: The practical use is building a palette where every step is perceptually even — lightening a brand colour in HSL shifts its apparent brightness, in OKLCH it does not. That is the fix for the 'why does our hover state look muddy' problem.
It shows the sRGB fallback alongside the P3 value, which is the part people skip: an OKLCH colour outside sRGB renders differently on older displays unless you ship the fallback.
Free tool from a consultancy, no account, nothing to depend on at runtime. Pair it with the APCA contrast guidance they link rather than WCAG 2 ratios.

entries.name: color.review
entries.what: Contrast checker that plots the whole range instead of returning one number — adjust foreground and background and it shows where the pair crosses 3:1, 4.5:1 and 7:1 for text and headlines, with a shareable URL per combination.
entries.priceDetail: Free, no account.
notes: Better than a pass/fail checker for the actual job, which is finding the nearest accessible version of a colour a client has already signed off. The curve shows you how far you have to move, not just that you failed.
URLs encode the pair (color.review/check/293845-FFFFFF), so an accessibility note in a PR or a client email can link to the evidence.
WCAG 2 contrast ratios only. For perceptual accuracy on light text or thin type, cross-check with APCA — the maths behind the 4.5:1 threshold is known to be wrong at the extremes.

entries.name: ray.so
entries.what: Turns a snippet of code into a shareable image — syntax themes, background on or off, dark or light window, padding control. Raycast's own tool, and the source is MIT on GitHub.
entries.priceDetail: Free. MIT licence (raycast/ray-so).
notes: The fastest route from a snippet to something presentable in a deck, a case study or a launch post — the alternative is a screenshot of an editor with someone's file tree in it.
MIT and self-hostable, which matters if we want a Gitwork-themed variant for case studies rather than Raycast's default palettes.
Nothing to depend on: it renders client-side and the output is a PNG or SVG we own.

entries.name: Screen Studio
entries.what: macOS screen recorder that applies automatic zoom on mouse actions and smooths the cursor path, so a raw capture comes out looking edited. Built for product demos and tutorials rather than meetings.
entries.priceDetail: $29/month billed monthly, or $9/month billed yearly. One plan, all features. macOS only — Ventura 13.1+ recommended.
notes: The automatic zoom and cursor smoothing is the entire product, and it is the difference between a demo video a client can put on a landing page and one that looks like a support call. $9/month on annual billing against half a day in an editor per video.
macOS only, so it is a personal-machine tool, not something we can put in a client's hands if they are on Windows.
No free tier listed on the pricing section — plan for the annual figure. Effectively a solo product (Adam Pietrasiak) with a long track record and Product Hunt #1 of the year.

entries.name: Raycast
entries.what: Extensible launcher replacing Spotlight — clipboard history, window management, snippets, script commands and a store of community extensions, with AI and cloud sync on the paid tier. Mac, plus a Windows beta.
entries.priceDetail: Free forever for individuals, including all built-in and community extensions. Pro $10/month monthly or $8/month annual (Raycast AI, unlimited notes, cloud sync, custom themes, translator). Team $15/user/month monthly or $12/user/month annual. Advanced AI add-on +$8/user/month.
notes: The free tier is genuinely the whole launcher — clipboard history and window management alone justify installing it, and nothing is time-limited. Pro buys AI and sync, not the core.
Worth standardising on because extensions are scriptable: a Raycast extension over Foundry's API would put client and task lookup a keystroke away on every machine.
Windows is still beta, so it cannot be the answer for a mixed-OS team yet. The free plan is licensed for organisational use, so there is no compliance reason to avoid it on work machines.

entries.name: Granola
entries.what: Meeting notepad that transcribes locally from the machine's audio rather than joining the call as a bot — you type sparse notes, it merges them with the transcript afterwards. Mac, Windows, mobile and an Apple Watch app.
entries.priceDetail: Basic $0/user/month: AI notes, limited meeting history, AI chat, shared folders, templates. Business $14/user/month: unlimited history, advanced models, integrations (Notion, Slack, HubSpot, Attio, Affinity, Zapier), MCP and API access. Enterprise $35/user/month for SSO and admin controls.
notes: No bot in the call is the point, and it is a client-facing point: nothing announces itself in a prospect meeting, and there is no second participant to consent to. Compare with what Scribe already does inside Foundry before adding another notes silo.
MCP and API access are Business-tier at $14/user/month — that is the tier if we ever want meeting context flowing into Foundry rather than sitting in Granola.

Recording a client call still needs their consent regardless of whether a bot appears; the tool removes the awkwardness, not the obligation. Model-training opt-out is available on every tier, including free.

entries.name: Wispr Flow
entries.what: System-wide voice dictation that rewrites as it goes — punctuation, filler removal and tone applied to speech across any app, in 100+ languages, learning names and jargon from use. Adds a meeting notetaker on Mac.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month: dictation across all apps, 100+ languages, Mac/Windows/iOS/Android, notetaker (Mac only), MCP access to notes, HIPAA-ready. Pro $15/user/month monthly or $12/user/month annual: unlimited dictations, longer meeting retention, advanced models. Enterprise on request.
notes: Where it pays off is prompting: dictating a long, specific brief to a coding agent is several times faster than typing it, and the cleanup is what separates this from built-in dictation.
The free tier caps dictation volume rather than features, so the real cost of adopting it across the team is $12/user/month on annual billing.

$81M raised and enterprise compliance claims (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001) — but everything dictated passes through their processing. Model-training opt-out exists on every tier; check it before dictating anything under a client NDA.

entries.name: LocalSend
entries.what: Cross-platform file transfer over the local network with no cloud, no account and no internet — Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, using an encrypted peer-to-peer connection between devices on the same Wi-Fi.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. No ads or trackers per the project's own claim.
notes: The practical case is AirDrop across an OS boundary: getting a build, a video or a set of assets from a Mac to an Android test device or a Windows machine without uploading a client's files to a third party.
Because it never leaves the local network, it is the safe answer for moving anything covered by an NDA between machines — no service to audit, no retention policy to read.
70k+ stars and 5M+ downloads claimed on the site. Open source with contributors rather than a company; a stalled release cycle costs nothing since the protocol is local.

entries.name: The Component Gallery
entries.takeaway: 60 interface components cross-referenced against 95 published design systems, with 2,671 concrete examples — so for any component you can read how Carbon, Polaris, Material and 90 others named it, structured it and what states they defined. Also lists the design systems themselves.
entries.whatToDo: Reference before naming or specifying a component. Action: when a client design system needs a component we have not built before, open its page here first and steal the naming and the state list rather than inventing them.
notes: The value is settling arguments cheaply: 'is it a Toast or a Snackbar, and does it need a dismiss action' becomes a five-second lookup across 95 systems instead of a meeting.
It is a reference index, not code — every example links out to someone else's documentation, so nothing here ships.
Maintained by one person (Iain Bean) and up to date at the time of adding. Worth screenshotting anything a client design system depends on.

entries.name: Easing Functions Cheat Sheet
entries.takeaway: Every standard easing curve — the ease-in/out/inOut families plus back, elastic and bounce — animated side by side with its graph, its cubic-bezier CSS value and its maths, so you can pick by watching rather than by name.
entries.whatToDo: Reference during motion work. Action: when a transition feels wrong, open this, find the curve that matches the intent, and paste the cubic-bezier value rather than nudging numbers.
entries.cost: Free. The site's own code is GPL-3.0.
notes: The reason to keep it to hand: naming is the problem in motion work — 'make it snappier' is unactionable, 'easeOutBack, 400ms' is a spec. This turns taste into a value you can put in a PR.
Copy the cubic-bezier values, not the site's source. The page code is GPL-3.0, which would be a licensing problem in a client repo; the curves themselves are just numbers.
Static reference, no dependency, nothing to break.

entries.name: Design Spells
entries.takeaway: A catalogue of individual delightful details captured from shipped products — easter eggs, transitions, confetti, Dynamic Island tricks, 404s — each tagged by type and platform (Mobile, Desktop, Interaction, Animation, Skeuomorphic). One detail per entry, not whole screens.
entries.whatToDo: Reference when a build needs one memorable moment. Action: pick a single spell to implement on the next Gitwork or client site rather than scattering effects across it.
entries.cost: Free. Newsletter and sponsor slots; no paywall.
notes: Useful precisely because it is granular: the entries are things a developer can implement in an afternoon, unlike a full-page inspiration shot that implies a redesign.
Run by two people (Chester and Duncan) with a newsletter attached — assume it can go quiet. Capture anything worth reusing rather than linking to it from internal docs.
Every entry is another product's craft. Take the idea and rebuild it; do not copy assets.

entries.name: 60fps.design
entries.takeaway: 2,024 screen recordings of interaction and animation detail from 475 best-in-class iOS and web apps, plus 77 app sites, 25 motion studies and a handful of code snippets. Recordings rather than stills, and it exposes an MCP endpoint so an agent can query the collection.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for motion specs. Action: when specifying a transition for a client build, find the closest recording here and attach it to the ticket — a video beats an adjective.
entries.cost: Free to browse. No pricing page published.
notes: The MCP endpoint is the interesting part and the reason this is worth knowing over the other inspiration sites: an agent implementing an interaction can pull real reference instead of guessing at timings.
No pricing page exists, so 'free' is the current state rather than a commitment — the collection may gate later.
Recordings of other companies' products. Fine as a motion spec, not as an asset source.

entries.name: Recent (formerly Godly)
entries.takeaway: Daily curation of exceptional websites, split into browsable sections for Websites, OG Images, App Screenshots, App Icons, Resources, Tools, Skills and Jobs, filtered by discipline (Interface, Branding, Typography, Motion, Editorial, Packaging). godly.website now redirects here.
entries.whatToDo: Reference at the start of a site project. Action: use the OG Images and App Icons sections specifically — those are the two assets we produce for every client and the two with the least reference material elsewhere.
entries.cost: Free to browse; account for saving. No pricing page published.
notes: The OG image and app icon sections are the genuinely differentiated bit. General website inspiration is oversupplied; a curated wall of 379 OG images is not.
Note the redirect: anything in our notes pointing at godly.website is now Recent, so the old bookmark is stale rather than dead.
3,498 members at the time of adding, with signups climbing fast — an early-stage curation site, so screenshot what matters.

entries.name: Saaspo
entries.takeaway: 3,097 SaaS pages broken down into 716 individual sections, plus 379 OG images and 46 templates, filterable so you can look at pricing sections or testimonial blocks in isolation rather than whole homepages.
entries.whatToDo: Reference when specifying a marketing site. Action: pull the relevant section type (pricing, feature grid, social proof) before writing the wireframe, so the structure argument happens against 20 shipped examples.
entries.cost: Free to browse; funded by sponsor slots. No pricing page (returns 404).
notes: Section-level filtering is what separates it from Awwwards-style galleries: our work is usually 'this pricing table is not converting', not 'redesign everything', and this indexes at that granularity.
Narrow to SaaS, which covers a good share of our client base and none of the rest.
Sponsor-funded with no pricing page — free today, no commitment. Other companies' pages, so structure-only input as ever.

entries.name: Cosmos
entries.takeaway: Visual reference tool where you build private connected collections and search across everything by colour or by visual similarity rather than by tag. Includes an AI-content filter with show, blur and hide settings, which no other reference library here offers.
entries.whatToDo: Reference management. Action: trial it against GatherOS for holding client mood boards, and turn the AI filter to hide when collecting craft references.
entries.cost: Free to join. Paid tiers are not published on any page we could read — the pricing route renders nothing without JavaScript.
notes: Search by colour and by visual similarity is the actual feature. Finding 'the reference with that exact green' across a year of saves is the thing tag-based tools cannot do.

The AI-content toggle matters more than it sounds: an inspiration library quietly filling with generated images is worthless for craft reference, and this is the only one here that lets you exclude it.
Pricing unverified — /pricing, /about and the help centre all render client-side and returned nothing readable, so assume a paid tier exists and check in-app before the team standardises on it.

entries.name: UNCUT.wtf
entries.takeaway: 163 contemporary typefaces, all free for commercial use, filtered by classification — 66 sans, 47 display, 27 serif, 23 monospace. Curated for current type rather than comprehensive, which is why the hit rate is high.
entries.whatToDo: Source fonts here before proposing a licensed family. Action: on the next brand or site project, shortlist from UNCUT first and check each font's own licence file before it reaches a client deliverable.
entries.cost: Free for commercial use. All fonts remain copyright of their respective creators.
notes: Directly saves client budget: a display face with real personality at no licence cost, and no per-domain webfont renewal to explain to a client three years later.

'Free for commercial use' is the catalogue's framing, but each typeface carries its own licence from its own designer. Read the individual licence before shipping — some restrict webfont use or redistribution even when the desktop file is free.
One curator, running since 2021. The fonts are downloaded files, so the catalogue disappearing costs us nothing already in a project.

entries.name: Fontshare
entries.takeaway: 100 font families from the Indian Type Foundry, free for personal and commercial use, with variable versions, OpenType feature listings and a web API for serving them. Professionally drawn families rather than a mixed catalogue — Satoshi, Switzer and General Sans come from here.
entries.whatToDo: First stop for a free workhorse sans or serif. Action: use the API's licence field to confirm each family before it ships, and self-host the files rather than hotlinking their CDN on a client site.
entries.cost: Free. Every family in their API carries license_type "itf_ffl" — the ITF Free Font Licence.
notes: The quality gap against most free catalogues is the point: these are foundry-drawn families with proper weights and OpenType features, so they hold up as a client's primary typeface rather than only as display type.

The licence page itself is JavaScript-only and did not render for us, so we have confirmed the licence type (itf_ffl) from their API but not read the terms. Read them before a client site depends on it.
One foundry behind all 100 families, which cuts both ways — consistent quality, single point of failure. Self-host the woff2 files in the repo.

entries.name: skills.sh
entries.takeaway: Leaderboard and installer for agent skills — `npx skills add owner/repo` pulls a skill into your agent, and the directory ranks skills by anonymous install telemetry from that CLI. Supports packs, which bundle public and private skills behind one install command. The CLI is open source at vercel-labs/skills.
entries.whatToDo: Action: publish the Foundry starters worth sharing as a skills pack, and check the leaderboard before writing a skill from scratch — install counts are a better signal of what actually works than a README.
notes: Packs are the directly useful bit for us: a private pack of Gitwork skills installed with one command on every machine and in every client repo, instead of copying .claude directories by hand.

The ranking is install telemetry, not review — popular is not the same as good, and a skill that installs into an agent gets to run instructions on our machines. Read any skill's source before adding it.
Vercel Labs project, so treat it as an experiment with a company behind it rather than a supported product.

entries.name: Radix UI
entries.what: The unstyled, accessible primitives shadcn/ui is built on — dialog, popover, select, dropdown and the rest, each handling focus trapping, keyboard interaction and ARIA, with no styling opinions. Also ships Themes, an Icons set and the Colors scales.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT. Maintained by WorkOS.
notes: Worth listing separately from shadcn/ui because it is the layer underneath: when a copied shadcn component behaves oddly on keyboard or screen reader, the answer is in Radix's docs, not shadcn's.
The accessibility work is the product. Focus management on a nested dialog, or type-ahead on a select, is a fortnight of subtle bugs to reimplement and the reason not to hand-roll these.
Backed by a funded company rather than a lone maintainer, which is unusual in this list and matters for anything a client depends on for years.

entries.name: Sonner
entries.what: One toast component for React, by Emil Kowalski — `npm install sonner`, render `<Toaster />` at the root, call `toast()` anywhere. Stacking, swipe-to-dismiss and promise states are handled.
entries.priceDetail: Free, MIT.
notes: It is the toast shadcn/ui itself now recommends, so standardising on it means an agent-written component and a hand-written one agree on how notifications work.
Narrow and finished — the promise API (`toast.promise`) covers the loading/success/error pattern that otherwise gets rebuilt badly on every project.
One maintainer, but it is a small MIT dependency with no service behind it, so the downside is vendoring it.

entries.name: dnd kit
entries.what: Drag-and-drop toolkit written in TypeScript — framework-agnostic core with first-class React, Vue, Svelte and Solid packages, plus sortable lists, custom sensors, modifiers and a plugin layer.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source.
notes: Drag-and-drop is the classic underestimate: pointer, touch and keyboard sensors, collision detection, auto-scroll and accessible announcements are months of work, and clients ask for reorderable lists constantly.
Keyboard sensors mean a sortable list is operable without a mouse, which is the difference between a feature and an accessibility complaint.
The rewrite splits into a framework-agnostic core with per-framework bindings, so a Vue or Svelte client project is no longer a reason to pick a different library.

entries.name: SVGL
entries.what: Library of brand logos as clean SVGs, categorised (AI 67, Adobe 56, Design 62, Database 23 and so on), with light and dark variants, a public API, a shadcn/ui registry entry and editor extensions.
entries.priceDetail: Free, open source, no account.
notes: Solves a job we do on nearly every client site — the logo wall, the integrations grid, the tech-stack strip — where the alternative is hunting press kits and tracing PNGs.
The API and the shadcn registry mean an agent building a logo section can fetch the real mark instead of inventing one.

Third-party trade marks. Fine for showing genuine integrations or clients; get permission before implying an endorsement, and check each brand's own guidelines for a logo you are putting in front of the public.

entries.name: Phosphor Icons
entries.what: Icon family in six weights — thin through to fill, plus duotone — designed as one system so a whole interface can shift weight without redrawing anything. By Helena Zhang and Tobias Fried, with React, Vue, Svelte, Flutter and web-component packages.
entries.priceDetail: Free, MIT.
notes: The six-weight system is the reason to choose it over Lucide or Heroicons: a dense dashboard and a marketing page can share an icon set and still look right, because weight carries the difference.
MIT, so unlike most icon sets there is nothing to check before it ships in a client deliverable or a Gitwork starter.

The browsing site needs JavaScript and served nothing readable without it, so the family was assessed from its own description and packages rather than by browsing the set. Open it in a browser to pick icons.

entries.name: Iconbuddy
entries.what: Search across 300,000+ icons from open-source sets in one place — Phosphor, Tabler, Material, Solar, Lucide and dozens more — recolour and resize in the browser, then export SVG, PNG, JSX or Base64. Figma, VS Code, Framer and Chrome plugins.
entries.priceDetail: Free search and download. Pro $6.99/month, $49.99/year, or $120 once for lifetime. Team from 3 seats × $39/year = $117/year.
notes: The value is the search across sets: finding the one icon that matches a client's existing set without installing five libraries to compare.

The icons themselves come from their original open-source projects and keep those licences — Iconbuddy sells the search and the export, not the artwork, so check the source set's licence for anything unusual.
$120 lifetime is the sane option if anyone here uses it weekly; the monthly is hard to justify against free browsing on the source sites.

entries.name: Thiings
entries.what: Collection of 10,000+ AI-generated 3D icons in a single consistent style — objects, tools, food, tech — downloadable individually or as the whole set with JSON metadata.
entries.priceDetail: Personal $0: individual downloads, non-commercial only, attribution required. Indie $49 lifetime for businesses under $200k/year revenue. Business $199 lifetime for over $200k. Enterprise above $2M/year or 50+ staff. Reselling the icons as assets is excluded on every tier.
notes: Read the licence before it touches client work. The free tier is non-commercial with attribution, and their own terms say that when you are buying on behalf of a client you pick the tier matching the client's revenue, not ours — so a big client's site needs the $199 tier even though we bought it.
One consistent 3D style across 10,000 objects is genuinely hard to source; the usual alternative is commissioning renders or accepting a mismatched stock set.
AI-generated artwork, so treat provenance as unsettled for anything a client will trade mark or put on packaging.

entries.name: unDraw
entries.what: Open-source SVG illustration collection by Katerina Limpitsouni — pick a hex colour on the site and every illustration recolours to it before download.
entries.priceDetail: Free, open licence, no attribution required.
notes: No attribution required is the differentiator against most free illustration sets, and it is what makes it usable on a client deliverable without a credits line.
The on-site recolour means a set can be pulled straight into a client's brand colour instead of arriving in someone else's purple.
So widely used that it reads as a placeholder to anyone in the industry. Fine for internal tools, empty states and prototypes; a poor choice for a brand-led marketing page.

entries.name: Storyset
entries.what: Customisable illustrations with an online editor — change colours, swap components and animate a scene, then export as static SVG or an animated asset. Themed sets for business, education, medical, technology and people, plus a Figma plugin.
entries.priceDetail: Free to use and download. Run by Freepik; attribution terms were not readable in the served page, so check the licence on the asset before it ships.
notes: The animation export is the part unDraw does not do — an animated empty state or onboarding step without opening After Effects.

Freepik's free assets normally require attribution unless you hold a subscription, and the licence page did not render for us. Confirm before putting one on a client site, because retro-fitting a credit line is awkward.
Same house-style problem as unDraw, more so. Rated Low deliberately: useful for speed on internal or throwaway work, not for anything brand-led.

entries.name: CleanShot X
entries.what: Screenshot and screen-recording app for Mac with the parts the built-in tool lacks — scrolling capture, annotation, self-timer, hidden desktop icons, OCR, and an upload that returns a shareable link.
entries.priceDetail: $29 one-time for the Mac app and 1GB cloud, keep it forever; updates optional at $19/year after the first year. App + Cloud Pro $8 per user/month billed annually, or $10/month monthly. 30-day money-back guarantee.
notes: The one-time $29 licence with optional renewal is unusually honest pricing, and it makes this the cheap default for every machine here — the app keeps working if you never renew.
Scrolling capture and annotation are the day-to-day wins: a full-page screenshot of a client site with callouts, in one pass, instead of stitching three images.
Different job from Screen Studio, which is for polished demo video. This is for the twenty captures a day that go into Slack, tickets and QA notes.

entries.name: Shottr
entries.what: Small, fast Mac screenshot app aimed at people who care about pixels — scrolling screenshots, OCR, annotation, and measurement tools for checking spacing and colour against a design. A 2.3MB download.
entries.priceDetail: Free to download and use; the site sells a licence via its Buy page, but no figure was present in the served pricing text.
notes: The measurement instruments are the reason it is here rather than CleanShot: measuring spacing straight off the screen is exactly the front-end QA loop when a build is drifting from the design.
2.3MB and native, so it is a reasonable thing to put on every machine even alongside CleanShot X.
Pricing unverified — free is what the download page offers, and the licence figure was not readable, so do not quote a cost from this listing.

entries.name: Xnapper
entries.what: Mac screenshot app that beautifies automatically — balanced padding, background, rounded corners and, notably, automatic redaction of detected emails and sensitive text before you share.
entries.priceDetail: One-time: Basic $29.99 (1 Mac), Personal $54.99 (2 Macs), Standard $79.99 (3 Macs), each with a year of updates and optional renewal at 40% off. Team $5 per device/month billed annually.
notes: Automatic redaction is the feature worth paying for on client work — screenshots of a staging environment routinely leak real customer emails into a Slack channel or a deck.
Overlaps heavily with CleanShot X at more than twice the price. Pick one; this wins only if the auto-redaction and instant beautifying matter more than scrolling capture and cloud links.
Per-device licensing means a laptop and a studio Mac need the $54.99 tier, not the $29.99.

entries.name: Cap
entries.what: Open-source Loom alternative for macOS, Windows and Linux. Instant Mode gives a shareable link in seconds; Studio Mode is a local editor with zoom and layout controls. Self-hostable, so recordings can stay on infrastructure you own.
entries.priceDetail: Free forever for personal use, unlimited local recordings. Desktop Licence $29/year, perpetual. Cap Pro $8.16 per user/month for the hosted side. Open source on GitHub and self-hostable.
notes: Self-hosting is the argument. A walkthrough of a client's admin panel recorded to Loom's servers is their data on a third party's infrastructure; the same recording on our own instance is not a conversation with their security team.
Cross-platform, unlike Screen Studio and CleanShot, so it is the one screen-recording answer we can give a client on Windows.
Free tier is genuinely usable for local recordings — the paid tiers buy hosted sharing and team features, not the recorder.

entries.name: Arcade
entries.what: Interactive product demos: capture a flow in the browser extension or desktop app and it becomes a clickable walkthrough rather than a video, with branching, CTAs, personalisation and an MCP endpoint. Also generates AI voiceovers and videos from the same capture.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month: unlimited AI demos, 1 published demo, 1 published video, 200 AI credits a month. Growth $42.50 per seat/month billed yearly ($50 monthly): branding, translations, branching, CTAs and insights. Enterprise on request.
notes: The pitch that matters for us is client-facing: an interactive demo of a build we shipped is a better case-study artefact than a video, because the reader drives it and it survives on a phone.
The free tier's one published demo makes it a trial, not a plan — real use starts at $42.50 a seat.
Demos are hosted by Arcade and embedded, so a case study built on it dies if the account lapses. Keep a video capture of anything that matters.

entries.name: Rotato
entries.what: 3D mockup generator for Mac — drop a screenshot or a live URL onto a device model, then rotate, light and animate it from any angle and export 4K stills or video. 30+ devices and 80+ ready-made templates.
entries.priceDetail: Free to download and use on any Mac. Paid plans are listed at $239/year and $861/year; the pricing page frames these against hiring a 3D artist rather than itemising what each tier includes, so confirm in-app before buying.
notes: Fills the app-store-screenshot and case-study-hero job: an animated device mockup of a client build, without opening Blender or buying a template pack that dates in a year.
The device library is the perishable part — a mockup on last year's iPhone reads as stale, and staying current is exactly what the subscription buys.
Pricing is the least clear of anything in this batch. The free tier is real and worth trying first; get the tier details in writing before it goes on a client budget.

entries.name: FontBase
entries.what: Font manager for Mac, Windows and Linux — activate and deactivate families without installing them system-wide, organise by collection, preview with your own text, and pull in Google Fonts directly.
entries.priceDetail: Core font management is free on all three platforms. The Awesome tier adds features from around $3/month.
notes: The practical case is per-project activation: a Mac with 400 client fonts installed slows every design app and pollutes every font menu. Activating only the families for the project in hand fixes that.
Cross-platform, which matters if anyone here works on Windows — most font managers are Mac-only.
It manages fonts, it does not license them. Keeping a client's licensed families organised does not make them ours to reuse on the next project.

entries.name: Velvetyne Type Foundry
entries.takeaway: A libre type foundry, not a catalogue — French collective releasing experimental typefaces under free licences, with the sources on GitLab, an In Use section showing where each face has shipped, and workshops and writing about the politics of type.
entries.whatToDo: Source display type here when a brand needs a face with a point of view. Action: check each family's licence file on GitLab (they vary) before it ships, and use the In Use section to see how a face behaves at real sizes.
notes: Different job from Fontshare and UNCUT: these are experimental, opinionated faces — the ones that make a brand look like it was designed rather than configured.
Sources on GitLab means a face can be modified for a client, which almost no commercial licence allows. That is a real capability if a brand needs a bespoke ligature or a missing glyph.
Licences vary per family and are not uniform across the foundry, so read the specific one. A collective rather than a company — pace of updates follows volunteers.

entries.name: Open Foundry
entries.takeaway: A decade-old curated showcase of open-source typefaces — Archivo, Work Sans, Aileron, Bluu Next, Terminal Grotesque and others — presented with their makers and specimen views rather than as a download grid.
entries.whatToDo: Use it to shortlist an open-source workhorse with a specimen you can actually judge. Action: pair it with Fontshare and UNCUT as the three free-type sources, and record which one a client's face came from in their brand doc.
notes: Curation is the value — it is a small set chosen for quality, which is the opposite of Google Fonts' thousands and much faster to decide from.
Open-source licences, so the same families can be self-hosted and modified without a webfont subscription to renew.
It showcases rather than hosts, so downloads land you on each project's own repo where the licence lives. Read it there.

entries.name: Realtime Colors
entries.what: Applies a palette and type pairing to a full dummy website in the browser and updates live as you change them — so a colour scheme is judged on a real page with real hierarchy instead of as swatches. Figma plugin and a VS Code theme editor.
entries.priceDetail: Free, no account.
notes: It answers the question swatches cannot: what a palette does to a whole page. Most palettes that die in review died because nobody saw them at page scale until it was built.
Sharing a URL of a live palette is a faster client conversation than a PDF of colour chips, and it removes the 'it looked different in the deck' argument.
Judgement aid, not an accessibility check. Run the pairs through color.review or an APCA tool before committing — a palette can look right here and still fail contrast.

entries.name: Conductor
entries.what: Runs several coding agents at once, each in its own isolated workspace, so parallel work does not collide in one checkout. Local workspaces on a Mac on the free tier; Conductor Cloud runs them in cloud sandboxes.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0: parallel agents in local workspaces on your Mac, bring your own model subscriptions and keys. Pro $50/month adds Conductor Cloud workspace hours, multiplayer, the API and teams up to 5. Teams $60/month per user above that.
notes: Directly relevant to how we already work: the constraint on running three Claude Code sessions is that they fight over one working tree, and isolated workspaces per agent is precisely that fix.
The free tier is local-only but complete for one machine, and you bring your own Claude subscription — so there is no second model bill to trial it.

Cloud sandboxes mean client code leaving our machines. Check what a client's contract says about third-party processing before pointing Conductor Cloud at their repo; the local tier avoids the question entirely.

entries.name: OpenCode
entries.what: Open-source terminal coding agent with a desktop build for macOS, Windows and Linux. Model-agnostic — ships with free models included and connects to Claude, GPT, Gemini or any provider you hold a key for.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. Model costs are whatever provider you point it at; some models are included at no cost.
notes: The reason to know it: it is the credible open-source answer to Claude Code, and being model-agnostic it is the fallback if a client forbids a specific vendor or we need a local model on sensitive work.
Being open source, its prompts and tool definitions are readable — genuinely useful reference when writing our own agent tooling in Foundry.
Not a reason to move off Claude Code for day-to-day work. List it as the second option, and try it on an internal project before it touches a client repo.

entries.name: CodeRabbit
entries.what: AI pull-request reviewer that comments line by line with context from the whole repo, offers one-click fixes, runs linters and SAST tools, and learns from how a team responds to its past reviews. Integrates with Jira and Linear.
entries.priceDetail: Pro $24/month per user billed annually. Pro Plus $48/month per user adds multi-repo analysis and custom pre-merge checks. CodeRabbit Security $40/month per user. Slack agent billed at $0.50 per agent minute. 14-day free trial, no card.
notes: The case for a studio is consistency: every PR gets the same review even when the person who would have caught it is on another project. It does not replace review, it stops the obvious things reaching a human.
$24 a seat is real money against Claude Code already reviewing diffs on request. Trial it on one repo and measure whether it catches things we did not before committing the team.
It reads every client repo you connect it to. That is a processor relationship needing checking against client contracts, and the reason the Security tier exists separately.

entries.name: Firecrawl
entries.what: Turns any URL or whole site into clean Markdown or structured JSON for an agent to consume — handles JavaScript rendering, crawling and extraction behind one API, with a search endpoint on top.
entries.priceDetail: Free 1,000 credits/month, 2 concurrent requests. Hobby $16/month (5,000 pages). Standard $83/month (100,000 pages, 50 concurrent). Growth $333/month (500,000). Scale $599/month (1,000,000). All billed yearly; extra credits sold on top. Open source.
notes: This is the thing we keep hand-rolling. Every audit and content migration starts with 'fetch these pages and give me the text', and the fiddly parts — JS rendering, rate limits, boilerplate stripping — are exactly what this sells.
Open source with a hosted tier, so a sensitive client crawl can run on our own infrastructure while everyday work uses the hosted API.
Free tier is 1,000 pages a month, which genuinely covers a small site audit. Watch the credit model on a large crawl — a 100k-page site is the $83 tier, not the $16.

entries.name: Exa
entries.what: Search API built for agents rather than people — semantic search over the live web returning full page contents, plus crawling and a deep-research endpoint, priced per request instead of per seat.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier to start, then usage-based — search priced per thousand results and contents per page, with published unit rates from around $0.01 per request. No seat licence.
notes: Relevant to Foundry rather than to client sites: an agent that needs current information — competitor pages, a client's own live site, a standard that changed — needs a search API, and general web search results are shaped for humans.
Usage pricing means a runaway agent loop is a bill, not a rate-limit error. Cap it before wiring it into anything automated.
Verified the pricing model but not the per-tier detail; the published rates are unit prices, so model expected volume before committing.

entries.name: Composio
entries.what: Gives an agent authenticated tool access to 1,000+ apps — Gmail, Slack, Notion, GitHub and the rest — handling OAuth on behalf of a user, sandboxed execution and parallel tool calls, so you do not build an integration per service.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month to start, then $29/month and $229/month tiers with per-execution rates around $0.25–$0.30 above the included volume.
notes: The hard part it sells is delegated auth: holding a user's Google or Slack credentials safely so an agent can act as them. That is the part we should not be building ourselves for Foundry.
It becomes a custodian of client and staff credentials for every app you connect. That is a security review before adoption, not after — and a reason to scope it to internal tools first.

Worth flagging: their homepage carries text addressed to AI agents reading the HTML, pointing at their signup flow. Harmless here, but it is a live example of why an agent browsing the web needs to treat page content as untrusted input rather than instructions.

entries.name: Steel
entries.what: Open-source browser infrastructure for agents — managed headless Chrome sessions over an API, with session reuse, proxies and captcha handling, driven from Puppeteer, Playwright or Selenium.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier, then plans at $30, $100 and $250/month. Open source and self-hostable.
notes: Where Firecrawl reads pages, this drives them — the option when a job needs a logged-in session or a form filled, which is most real client migrations.
Open source and self-hostable, so a client's credentials need not sit in a third party's browser session.
Same note as Composio: the site embeds a line addressed to AI agents pointing at its setup instructions. Read it as marketing aimed at crawlers, not as guidance to follow.

entries.name: TinyPNG
entries.what: Image compression in the browser for WebP, AVIF, JXL, PNG and JPEG, with format conversion, a website analyser that estimates the savings available on any URL, and a developer API for automating it in a build.
entries.priceDetail: Free in the browser for everyday batches. The developer API is metered, with a free monthly allowance before paid usage.
notes: Still the fastest fix for the most common client complaint we get about performance — a 4MB hero image someone exported from Figma at full size.
The site analyser is the useful half for us: point it at a client's live URL and get a number for the savings, which is a better argument in a report than 'optimise your images'.
Next.js and Vercel already optimise images at build and request time, so this is for assets outside that pipeline — email, decks, uploads to a CMS — rather than for the app itself.

entries.name: Dropover
entries.what: Mac drag-and-drop shelf: shake the pointer mid-drag and a floating tray appears to hold files, links, text or images, so you can gather from several places and drop them all at once instead of one window at a time.
entries.priceDetail: Free to download and use.
notes: Small but constant: collecting assets from four folders into a client upload, or pulling files out of a download folder into a project, is a daily task and macOS makes it needlessly fiddly.
Native and unobtrusive — it appears only when you shake mid-drag, so it costs nothing when unused.
Handles files, links, text and images in one shelf, which makes it a staging area for a deck or a handover rather than only a file mover.

entries.name: Open Source Alternative To
entries.takeaway: 505 open-source alternatives to proprietary products, each listed against the product it replaces with its GitHub star count and category — Godot for Unity, and equivalents across analytics, CRM, forms, storage and design.
entries.whatToDo: Open it when a client baulks at a SaaS line item or needs data on their own infrastructure. Action: check it before proposing a paid tool in a scope of work, so the open alternative is a considered choice rather than an oversight.
notes: Directly useful in proposals: 'the open-source equivalent is X, self-hosted, and here is what it costs to run' is a stronger position than only quoting the SaaS.
Star counts are the only quality signal it carries — popularity is not maintenance. Check commit recency and licence on anything before recommending it to a client.
Self-hosting moves cost from a subscription to our time. Say that plainly when proposing one, or it lands as a saving that later becomes a support burden.

entries.name: Cursor
entries.what: VS Code fork built around agents — tab completion, inline edits and a background agent that takes a task and returns a diff, with the whole repo as context.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Pro $20/month. Teams $40/user/month. Heavy agent use bills usage above the included allowance.
notes: The default paid editor for most people writing code with AI, and the one a new developer here will already know. Worth listing even though it is obvious, because the alternative is pretending our stack is more exotic than it is.
Usage billing on top of $20 is the part that surprises people. Watch it on a month of heavy agent work.
It reads whole client repos. Check the privacy mode setting before opening work under an NDA.

entries.name: Cline
entries.what: Open-source coding agent that runs inside VS Code with explicit Plan and Act modes — it proposes a plan, you approve, then it executes with terminal and MCP access.
entries.priceDetail: Free, Apache 2.0. You pay whichever model provider you point it at.
notes: The Plan/Act split is the useful idea: an agent that shows its plan before touching files is far easier to supervise on client work than one that starts editing.
Apache 2.0 and bring-your-own-key, so there is no vendor holding the workflow and no second subscription — useful when a client insists on a specific model or region.
Claims 8M+ developers on its own site. Treat that as marketing, but the project is genuinely active and MCP support is first-class.

entries.name: Aider
entries.what: Terminal-based pair programmer that edits files in a git repo and commits each change with a sensible message, so every agent edit is a reviewable commit rather than a mystery diff.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. Model costs are your own API keys.
notes: The git-native design is the reason to know it: one commit per change means `git log` is the audit trail of what the agent did, which is exactly what a client handover needs.
Terminal-only, no editor integration — that is the point on a server or in CI, and a limitation on a designer's machine.
Model-agnostic and mature. A reasonable fallback if a client forbids the vendors we normally use.

entries.name: Bolt.new
entries.what: Prompt-to-app in the browser: describe a site or app and it scaffolds, runs and previews a full stack in a WebContainer, with deploy from the same page.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier with limited tokens. Paid plans from $25/month, with a $30 tier above it.
notes: Genuinely fast for a throwaway prototype in a pitch — a working clickable thing in the meeting beats a wireframe.
Everything runs in the browser sandbox, so what you get out is a starting point, not a codebase we would hand to a client without rewriting.
Token-metered, so an afternoon of iteration can burn a month's allowance. Prototype, export, then build properly.

entries.name: v0
entries.what: Vercel's generative UI tool — describe an interface and it returns React and Tailwind using shadcn/ui components, iterating in a chat with a live preview, then deploys to Vercel.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0/month with limited credits. Premium $30/user/month, with usage credits beyond the allowance and a $100/user enterprise tier.
notes: It outputs shadcn/ui and Tailwind, which is the stack we already use — so unlike most generators the output lands in our codebase rather than beside it.
Best used for the first pass on a component or a marketing section, then edited by hand. The generated markup is verbose and rarely accessible without a pass.
Same company as our hosting, so the deploy path is short. That is convenience, not lock-in worth worrying about at this size.

entries.name: Replit
entries.what: Browser IDE with hosting, databases and an agent that builds and deploys a working app from a description — the whole loop in one tab, no local setup.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid plans from $20/month, with a $25 tier and higher usage-based plans up to around $100/month.
notes: The zero-setup part is the real value for us: handing a client or a non-developer a running environment they can poke at, without an install call.
Agent usage is metered on top of the subscription, and it moves fast on a big build.
For anything we ship, code belongs in our own repo on our own pipeline. Treat Replit as a sketchpad, not a home.

entries.name: Builder.io
entries.what: Visual development platform that turns Figma frames into React, Vue or Svelte components against your existing design system, plus a headless CMS so marketers can edit published pages without a deploy.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid plans at $24 and $40/month, with usage-based tiers above.
notes: The pitch that matters on retainer work: a client's marketing team edits pages themselves instead of sending us a ticket to change a headline.
Design-to-code output still needs review — mapping to an existing component library is the hard part and it is only as good as the mapping you configure.
It becomes part of the client's publishing pipeline, so removing it later is a migration. Scope that before proposing it.

entries.name: Subframe
entries.what: Visual UI builder that edits real React components rather than a canvas of shapes — drag a layout together from your own design system and it emits production React and Tailwind, with an MCP endpoint for agents.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $29/month.
notes: Closer to how we actually work than Figma-to-code: the source of truth is components, so the output is not a fresh pile of divs each time.
The MCP endpoint means an agent can build against the real design system instead of inventing markup — the same argument as 21st.dev, applied to layout.
Young product. Worth a trial on an internal build before a client depends on it.

entries.name: Magic Patterns
entries.what: Prompt-to-prototype tool aimed at product teams — generates UI in React from a description or an image, can be pointed at your design system, and shares as an interactive prototype.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier; paid plans are not published in the served pricing page, so check in-app before committing.
notes: Overlaps with v0. The distinction is that it aims at a shareable prototype for a product conversation rather than at code you keep.
Design-system binding is the feature worth testing — untethered generation is a demo, not a workflow.
Pricing unverified from the site; do not quote a figure from this listing.

entries.name: Kiro
entries.what: AWS's agentic IDE built around spec-driven development — a prompt becomes an executable spec with requirements and design docs, and the agent works against that rather than against a chat history.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid from $20/month, with $40, $100 and $200 tiers and per-request overage around $0.04.
notes: The spec-first idea is the interesting part and matches how we already brief agents in Foundry — a written spec the agent is held to beats a long chat.
AWS backing means it will not disappear, and it will pull toward AWS services. Worth knowing which of those assumptions land in generated code.
Another editor to learn. Only worth the switch if spec-driven working proves better on a real project than our current setup.

entries.name: Devin
entries.what: Autonomous coding agent that runs in its own cloud environment and works asynchronously — you assign an issue, it plans, writes, tests and opens a pull request, with several agents running in parallel.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier to try. Paid from $20/month, with a $200/month plan and per-seat pricing around $40–$80/month at team scale.
notes: The async model is the difference from Claude Code: work is handed off and collected later rather than supervised live, which suits backlog chores more than design-led work.
Pricing came down a long way from its original $500/month. It is now a plausible experiment rather than an enterprise-only line item.
Autonomy is the risk, not the feature. Give it well-specified, low-blast-radius work and review every PR properly.

entries.name: Greptile
entries.what: AI pull-request reviewer that indexes the whole codebase first, so its comments reference how the repo actually does things rather than reading the diff in isolation.
entries.priceDetail: $30 per seat/month, with usage-based components around $1–$2 per unit above the allowance. Free trial available.
notes: Whole-repo indexing is the claim that separates it from a diff-only reviewer — the bugs that matter are usually about a convention elsewhere in the codebase.
Direct competitor to CodeRabbit at a similar price. Trial both on the same repo before picking; do not run both.
Indexing a client repo means a full copy on their infrastructure. That needs checking against the client contract.

entries.name: Qodo
entries.what: Code quality suite — generates tests from existing code, reviews pull requests, and ships agentic workflows into the IDE and CI, with the emphasis on test coverage rather than style comments.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid around $30/user/month.
notes: The test-generation half is the useful bit for us: our weak spot on fast client builds is coverage, not review, and generated tests at least pin current behaviour before a refactor.
Generated tests can enshrine a bug as expected behaviour. They are a safety net for refactoring, not a substitute for thinking about the cases.
Overlaps with CodeRabbit and Greptile on review. Pick one lane.

entries.name: Tabby
entries.what: Self-hosted, open-source coding assistant — runs the model on your own hardware so completions never leave the network, with an admin layer for teams.
entries.priceDetail: Open source and free to self-host. Hosted and supported plans from $19/month, with annual tiers at $180, $280 and $480/year.
notes: This is the answer to a client who will not allow code to leave their network — a real constraint on public-sector and finance work, and one we currently have no answer for.
Self-hosting means running a GPU box and owning the uptime. Price that as our time before offering it.
Completion quality trails the frontier hosted models. It buys compliance, not capability.

entries.name: Mintlify
entries.what: Documentation platform that publishes from Markdown in a repo, keeps itself updated from code changes, and serves docs in a form agents can consume as well as people.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid plans metered, with usage priced from around $0.01 per unit.
notes: Docs are the thing that rots first on a client handover. Publishing from the repo at least keeps them next to the code that changed.
The agent-readable angle is becoming the point: a client's own agents will read their docs, and badly structured docs now cost twice.
We could build this with Next.js and MDX in a fortnight, and have. The question is whether maintaining it beats paying for it.

entries.name: Vercel
entries.what: The hosting and build platform this site runs on — preview deploys per branch, edge network, serverless and analytics, with first-class Next.js support.
entries.priceDetail: Hobby $0/month. Pro $20/month per user, with usage-based charges for bandwidth, functions and image optimisation on top.
notes: Listed because it is the default deploy target for everything we build, and because preview deploys per pull request are the single biggest thing that speeds up client review.
Usage billing is the trap: a client site with heavy image traffic can cost far more than the $20 seat suggests. Model it before quoting hosting.
Their Open Source Program, already on this list, covers credits for qualifying projects.

entries.name: Figma
entries.what: The design tool the industry standardised on — multiplayer canvas, components and variables, dev mode for handoff, and Make for generating working prototypes from a prompt.
entries.priceDetail: Free starter. Paid seats from $3/month for viewers and $12–$16/month for full seats, with $25 and $55/month tiers for dev and organisation plans.
notes: Listed for completeness rather than discovery: it is where client work starts, and the seat model is what makes a client's costs jump when they add reviewers.
Variables and dev mode are the parts under-used on our projects — they are what makes a design system survive contact with code.
The alternative worth knowing is Penpot, already on this list, for a client who will not put IP in Figma.

entries.name: Framer
entries.what: Design tool and host in one — build a site on a canvas with real CSS layout, add a CMS and analytics, and publish to their hosting. Now with an agent that designs and builds on the canvas.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0. Paid site plans from $10/month, with $30 and $40/month tiers, plus $20/month per additional editor seat.
notes: The right answer for a marketing site that a client will edit themselves and we do not want to maintain — faster than Next.js and cheaper to hand over.
The line to hold: Framer for brochure sites, our own stack for anything with real product logic. Mixing them mid-project is where budgets go.
Sites live on Framer's hosting, so an export is not a clean migration path. Say that to the client before, not after.

entries.name: Webflow
entries.what: Visual web builder producing real HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with a proper CMS, staging, and an interactions layer for scroll and hover animation without code.
entries.priceDetail: Free to build. Site plans from around $6/month for basic sites, with business and enterprise tiers running to $200–$500/month at scale.
notes: The main alternative to Framer for client marketing sites, with a stronger CMS and a much larger pool of freelancers who can maintain it after we hand over.
Its pricing splits between workspace seats and per-site plans, which reliably confuses clients on a first invoice. Explain both.
Heavier and less pleasant to design in than Framer; better when the content model is genuinely complex.

entries.name: Excalidraw
entries.what: Hand-drawn-style virtual whiteboard, free and open source, with no signup — diagrams look deliberately sketchy, which keeps a client conversation about structure rather than styling.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. A paid Excalidraw+ tier exists for teams and hosted collaboration.
notes: The sketchy aesthetic is a feature: nobody argues about corner radius on an architecture diagram that looks hand-drawn, so the discussion stays on the system.
No signup means it works instantly on a call with a client who has never used it — the lowest-friction option here alongside tldraw.
Diagrams live in a file you own and can commit next to the code. That matters for handover docs.

entries.name: Eraser
entries.what: Diagram-as-code tool for technical docs — write a description or prompt it and get architecture, sequence and ERD diagrams that live in version control alongside the docs they illustrate.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid plans at $15 and $20/month per user, with $45 and $60/month team tiers.
notes: Diagram-as-code is the reason to prefer it over a canvas for handover docs: the diagram updates in a pull request rather than rotting in someone's Figma file.
Mermaid does much of this for free and renders natively in GitHub and our own artifacts. Try that before paying.
Useful specifically for the architecture section of a client handover, which is the document most likely to be wrong six months later.

entries.name: Napkin
entries.what: Turns written text into explanatory graphics — paste a paragraph and it proposes diagrams, flows and comparisons, editable afterwards, aimed at decks and documents rather than engineering diagrams.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $9/month and $22/month.
notes: The practical use is proposals and reports: a diagram per section, generated from the text we already wrote, instead of a wall of prose.
Output is generic by default. It needs restyling to our brand before anything goes to a client, which removes much of the speed.
$9/month is cheap against the hour it saves per document, if anyone actually adopts it.

entries.name: Google Stitch
entries.what: Generates mobile and web UI from a text prompt or a reference image, returning both a visual design and front-end code, then exports to Figma. Google's successor to Galileo AI.
entries.priceDetail: Free, with a Google account.
notes: Free is the differentiator against Uizard and Visily. For a first-pass concept in a pitch, cost per idea matters more than polish.
The Figma export makes it a starting point rather than a dead end — the output can be taken into a real design process.
Worth knowing that usegalileo.ai now redirects here: Galileo AI was acquired by Google and became Stitch, so older bookmarks and directory listings for Galileo are stale.

entries.name: Uizard
entries.what: Wireframing and mockup tool aimed at non-designers — generates screens from a prompt, converts a hand-drawn sketch or screenshot into an editable design, and produces clickable prototypes.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Pro $12/month, Business $39/month.
notes: Rated Low deliberately: we have designers, so generated wireframes save us little. Its value is letting a client sketch their own idea before a kickoff.
The screenshot-to-editable-design path is the genuinely useful trick, for taking apart a competitor's flow.
Output is not close to production quality and should never be shown as our work.

entries.name: Khroma
entries.what: Colour tool trained on your own choices — pick fifty colours you like once, and it then generates palettes, gradients and type pairings filtered to that taste, searchable by name or hex.
entries.priceDetail: Free, with an account for the training step.
notes: The training step is what makes it different from every other palette generator: results are filtered to a taste rather than to a colour-wheel rule.
